title: Hundredths
keyIdea: Cut one tenth into 10 equal parts and each part is one hundredth of the whole, written 1/100 or 0.01. Ten hundredths make one tenth, so after 0.09 the count goes on to 0.1, and 100 hundredths make 1 whole. A decimal like 0.37 means 3 tenths and 7 hundredths, which is 37 hundredths. Dividing 1 by 100, or a tenth by 10, gives a hundredth; a centimetre is a hundredth of a metre. To compare decimals, write both in hundredths: 0.4 is 40 hundredths, so it is bigger than 0.35.

kid: Cut a cake into 10 equal slices. Each slice is one tenth. Now cut one slice into 10 tiny bits. Each bit is one hundredth of the cake.
We write one hundredth as 1/100 or 0.01. The second place after the dot shows hundredths.
Count in hundredths: 0.07, 0.08, 0.09. Next comes 10 hundredths. That is the same as one tenth, so we write 0.1.
0.4 looks short, but it is 4 tenths. That is 40 hundredths. So 0.4 is bigger than 0.35, which is 35 hundredths.
adult: In the National Curriculum for England, Year 4 pupils count up and down in hundredths. They recognise that hundredths arise when dividing an object by 100 and dividing tenths by 10. They write decimal equivalents of any number of tenths or hundredths, and divide one- or two-digit numbers by 10 and 100. This lesson builds on the Year 3 tenths lesson.

The key link is that the hundredths place is ten times smaller than the tenths place. A hundred square shows it well: each column is a tenth and each small square is a hundredth. So 0.37 is 3 columns and 7 squares, which is 37 hundredths. Metric length gives a real context, since 1 cm = 0.01 m.

Common mistakes: thinking a longer decimal is larger (0.35 > 0.4 because 35 > 4), writing 7 hundredths as 0.7, and counting 0.08, 0.09, 0.010 instead of 0.1. Some children treat the digits after the point as a separate whole number. Writing both numbers in hundredths, so 0.4 becomes 0.40, fixes most of these.

In the lab your child cuts a tenth of a hundred square into 10, counts from 3/100 to 12/100 on a number line, and shades 37 hundredths. Then they stretch a ribbon to 0.25 m on a metre stick and shade 0.4 and 0.35 side by side to compare them.

familyTip: Use a tape measure: 1 cm is one hundredth of a metre. Measure a spoon or a shoe and say it both ways, such as 23 cm and 0.23 m. Money works too, since 1p is a hundredth of £1, so 45p is £0.45. Ask which is more, 0.5 m or 0.45 m, and check on the tape.

practice.prompt: How many hundredths are there in {a} tenths?
practice.hint: One tenth is 10 hundredths, like one column of a hundred square.
practice.explain: Each tenth is 10 hundredths, so {a} tenths = {a} × 10 = {=a*10} hundredths.

practice.prompt: {a} tenths and {b} hundredths make how many hundredths in all?
practice.hint: Change the tenths into hundredths first, then add the extra hundredths.
practice.explain: {a} tenths = {=10*a} hundredths. Add {b} more: {=10*a+b} hundredths, written 0.{a}{b}.

practice.hint: Write both as hundredths. 0.7 is 7 tenths.
practice.explain: 0.7 = 70 hundredths and 0.65 = 65 hundredths. 70 > 65, so 0.7 is bigger even though it has fewer digits.

practice.prompt: A ribbon is 0.{a}{b} m long. How many centimetres is that?
practice.hint: 1 cm is one hundredth of a metre.
practice.explain: 0.{a}{b} m is {=10*a+b} hundredths of a metre, and each hundredth of a metre is 1 cm, so it is {=10*a+b} cm.

practice.hint: How many hundredths make one tenth?
practice.explain: 9 + 1 = 10 hundredths, and 10 hundredths make 1 tenth, so the answer is 0.1. 0.010 is only 1 hundredth.

pool.prompt: How do you write 7 hundredths as a decimal?
pool.hint: Hundredths go in the second place after the point.
pool.explain: 0.07 has 0 tenths and 7 hundredths. 0.7 would be 7 tenths, which is 70 hundredths.

pool.prompt: Start at {a} hundredths and count on {b} more hundredths. How many hundredths do you have?
pool.hint: Count on one hundredth at a time. Remember that 10 hundredths make 1 tenth.
pool.explain: {a} + {b} = {=a+b} hundredths. That is 1 tenth and {=a+b-10} hundredths, because 10 hundredths make one tenth.

pool.hint: 0.5 is 5 tenths. Change the tenths into hundredths.
Dividing by 100 makes a number 100 times smaller.
pool.explain: 4 ÷ 100 = 4 hundredths = 0.04. Each digit moves two places to the right. 0.4 would be 4 ÷ 10.

pool.prompt: A pencil is 0.{a} m long. How many centimetres is that?
pool.hint: 0.{a} m is {a} tenths of a metre. How many hundredths is that?
pool.explain: 0.{a} m = {a} tenths of a metre = {=10*a} hundredths of a metre = {=10*a} cm.
In hundredths they are 30, 29 and 31. 29 is the smallest, so 0.29 is the smallest.

pool.hint: One more hundredth makes 100 hundredths. How much is that?
pool.explain: 0.99 + 0.01 = 100 hundredths, which is 1 whole. 0.100 is only 1 tenth.

pool.prompt: Mia says 0.45 is bigger than 0.5 because 45 is bigger than 5. Is she right?
choices: No, 0.5 is 50 hundredths, so it is bigger
pool.hint: Write both numbers in hundredths before comparing.
pool.explain: 0.5 = 0.50 = 50 hundredths, and 0.45 = 45 hundredths. 50 > 45, so 0.5 is bigger.
